reviews.response:
Referee verdict: ACCEPT for the general residual theorem; exact applications require source-level qualificationsThe central residual compensation inequality is mathematically sound. In particular, the use of
$$\boxed{b_R+\max\{C_s,J_d\}}$$
rather than the sum is correct. The HH maximum-flow quantity is used in the correct direction: it is an upper bound on how many of the demanded arrivals can be supplied for free, and therefore produces a lower bound on the number of compulsory TH arrivals.There is, however, an important distinction between three claims:The abstract lower-bound theorem.The physical realization of its min-cost path relaxation.The exactness of a constructed full completion.The first two have a convincing proof under the stated graph conventions. The third is a conditional certificate theorem, not an unconditional optimizer theorem. The two numerical applications also need their finite geometric data independently established; the supplied manuscript does not itself provide enough of the earlier source definitions to certify every coordinate-level assertion.1. General theorem: proof auditLet  $N$  be any full matching retaining  $R$ . Write  $P_N$  for its residual terminal paths. The argument has two independent lower-bound mechanisms.1.1 Endpoint Hall deficitThe terminal paths induce a bijection
$$T'\sqcup W'\longrightarrow B'.$$
For any  $D\subseteq B'$ , precisely  $|D|$  distinct sources are paired to destinations in  $D$ .At most  $|F|$  of these sources belong to  $F=N_{T'}(D)$ . Consequently at least
$$d=\max(0,|D|-|F|)$$
sources belong to  $U\sqcup W'$ .Select  $d$  of these paths. Their endpoint pairs constitute a matching in the assignment graph defining  $J_d$ . For each selected TH path, the shortest-path cost is no greater than its actual expense; for each HH path the assignment cost is zero.Therefore
$$f(N)-b_R\geq J_d.$$
This argument correctly preserves the distinction between endpoint matching and physical path disjointness. In particular, it does not require the assignment paths to have disjoint interiors.Correct The quantifier is over every full matching retaining all of  $R$ , not just a selected family of compensating paths.1.2 Physical HH capacity and compulsory TH compensationAmong the  $d$  selected arrivals, at most  $h_D$  can be HH: indeed, all HH paths ending in  $D$  in the actual completion constitute a feasible family in the physical HH maximization problem.Hence at least
$$s=\max(0,d-h_D)$$
of the selected paths must be TH.Moreover, at most  $|F|$  paths ending in  $D$  can start in  $F$ . Thus the compulsory TH paths can be chosen to start in  $U$ .They are physically vertex-disjoint, so they are feasible for the optimization defining  $C_s$ . Their total actual expense is at least  $C_s$ . Therefore
$$f(N)-b_R\geq C_s.$$
Combining the two inequalities gives
$$\boxed{
f(N)\geq b_R+\max\{C_s,J_d\}.
}$$
Taking the minimum over all retaining completions proves (2).The HH direction is correct. This is an especially important point. One does not need to prove that the independently optimized HH flow can coexist with an independently optimized TH flow. One needs only the fact that no actual completion can use more than  $h_D$  HH arrivals into  $D$ .The proof uses exactly that fact.1.3 Why the physical flow is genuinely vertex-disjointThe unusual feature of this network is that it does not assign independent capacities to the two endpoints of an actual matching edge.This is correct.For every actual edge  $e=(w,b)\in M'$ , the orientation is
$$b\longrightarrow w.$$
Every path entering the black endpoint  $b\in P'$  must leave it through this actual arc: it is the unique outgoing arc. Every path entering the white endpoint  $w\in P'$  must have entered through this same actual arc: it is the unique incoming arc.Consequently, capacity one on this single arc prevents either endpoint from being used by two different paths.Auxiliary arcs also have unit capacity. Source and sink terminal capacities prevent reuse of residual terminals.Thus every integral flow decomposes, after removal of circulations, into genuinely vertex-disjoint alternating paths. Conversely every such path family defines an integral flow.Nonnegative actual weights justify discarding circulations without increasing cost.Correct The physical-capacity argument is valid; replacing it with independently capacitated copies of actual-edge endpoints would not be an equivalent construction.1.4 The use of maximum, not sumThe two lower bounds are
$$f(N)-b_R\geq C_s,\qquad
f(N)-b_R\geq J_d.$$
They concern the same expense, not disjoint expense budgets.Therefore their combination is the maximum.The manuscript explicitly recognizes this and gives the appropriate warning about the 8-by-12 example.This is not merely a conservative presentation choice. Adding the two quantities would be mathematically unjustified.2. Attaining-completion criterionThe construction in Section 3 is sound, with one clarification concerning its logical scope.Take an optimal physical family of  $s$  TH paths attaining  $C_s$ , all starting in  $U$  and ending in  $D$ . Add those paths to  $R$ .Delete their vertices. On the remaining graph, forbid auxiliary edges from every remaining selected white terminal to every black  $P$ -vertex.Suppose the remaining graph has a perfect matching.Then:The prescribed paths remain intact.The remaining matching completes the original graph.Every remaining TH path is direct.Every remaining direct TH path has zero actual-edge expense.The remaining HH paths incur no TH expense, irrespective of the weights of their actual edges.The resulting full matching has expense exactly
$$b_R+C_s.$$
Now apply the general lower bound:
$$b_R+\max(C_s,J_d)
\leq f_R^*
\leq b_R+C_s.$$
It follows automatically that
$$J_d\leq C_s,\qquad
\boxed{f_R^*=b_R+C_s.}$$
This proves something slightly stronger than the stated conditional criterion: successful extension itself implies the required comparison  $C_s\geq J_d$ .The condition  $C_s\geq J_d$  is therefore redundant when the extension test succeeds and the general theorem is available.Required clarificationThe matching test is existential over a particular optimal physical path family. Failure for one chosen optimizer does not imply failure for another optimizer, and failure for every optimizer would still not establish general infeasibility of retaining  $R$ .The manuscript already acknowledges the first limitation. I recommend making the quantifiers explicit:
$$\exists P\in\operatorname{Opt}(C_s):
\quad
\operatorname{DirectRemainder}(R\cup P)
\text{ has a perfect matching}.$$
This is a sufficient exactness certificate, not a characterization of all unrestricted minimum-cost completions.There is no defect in the construction itself.3. The 8-by-12 retained-pair applicationThe numerical argument has the correct structure:
$$d=1,\quad h_D=0,\quad s=1,$$
and the claimed costs are
$$b_R=2,\qquad C_s=J_d=2.$$
Consequently the theorem yields
$$f_R^*\geq 2+\max(2,2)=4.$$
A successful direct-remainder matching gives the reverse inequality, hence
$$\boxed{f_R^*=4.}$$
This is consistent with the stated unrestricted optimum of two. The retained-path constraint costs an additional two.The displayed compensation path has six vertices and five edges:
$$(0,11),(1,11),(2,11),(3,11),(3,10),(4,10).$$
It has the required alternating length, with two actual edges and three auxiliary edges, provided the stated board matching assigns the second and fourth edges as actual edges.Referee qualification: I have not independently recovered the original RETAINING_PAIR_EXACT_UNIT_COST.md matching and adjacency tables in this session. The separately accepted fixed-board exact-four result is not a substitute for independently checking the new application’s identification of  $D,F,U$ , the path's edge types, and the successful remainder matching.Thus I accept the reduction of this example to the residual theorem, conditional on those previously established board facts; I do not represent the coordinate-level application as newly independently verified.4. The 12-by-18 all- $K$  constructionThis is the more important stress test because it checks whether the same HH source is inadvertently credited twice.4.1 Hall arithmeticThe claimed residual data are
$$\begin{array}{c|ccc}
 & |D|&|F|&d\\ \hline
D_0&17&16&1\\
\{h_0\}&1&0&1\\
D_0\cup\{h_0\}&18&16&2.
\end{array}$$
With the single residual HH source,
$$h_{D_0}=h_{\{h_0\}}=h_{D_0\cup\{h_0\}}=1.$$
The resulting compulsory TH counts are
$$s(D_0)=0,\qquad
s(\{h_0\})=0,\qquad
s(D_0\cup\{h_0\})=1.$$
This is exactly the intended competition phenomenon.The separate tests cannot establish a positive TH compensation cost, but the union test can.There is a small coordinate-counting clarification worth including in the text: the displayed coordinate union defining  $D_0$  contains 18 black checkerboard positions before accounting for the selected entrance  $(6,15)$ . The stated 17 is the residual count after that entrance is removed. The deletion convention should be stated next to the table.4.2 Lower boundFor the union,
$$d=2,\qquad h_D=1,\qquad s=1.$$
Every completion must therefore have at least one TH path from  $U$  to the union.Because  $U=T'\setminus F$ , this path cannot be direct. It must use at least one residual actual edge. All such edges have weight  $K$ , so
$$C_s\geq K.$$
The manuscript claims a path attaining that cost, hence
$$C_s=K.$$
Likewise, the endpoint assignment can pair one HH source at zero cost and one TH source at cost  $K$ , giving
$$J_d=K.$$
Thus
$$\boxed{f_R^*\geq 2+K.}$$
This is a genuine consequence of the union deficit. It does not rely on adding the two separate regional inequalities.4.3 Audit of the explicit completion countsThe displayed path data are internally consistent at the level of edge counts.PathVerticesEdgesAuxiliary edgesActual edges $A$ 4321 $C$ 4321 $T_0$ 4321HH path181798Total30261511The HH path's eight actual edges have no TH liability. This is an essential feature, not an accounting exception.The remaining direct matching counts also add up:
$$42+26=68.$$
The horizontal intervals have total cardinality 52, hence provide 26 horizontal matching edges. The listed vertical columns give 42 vertical edges.The final edge count is
$$15+25+42+26=108,$$
exactly the number of edges in a perfect matching of a 216-vertex bipartite board.There is also a useful independent vertex-count check:
$$30+2(68)+2(25)=216.$$
Thus the arithmetic is coherent.Terminology correction required: the 25 retained unused actual edges should be called common actual/auxiliary matching edges or doubled common edges, not simply auxiliary edges. They belong to  $M\cap N$ , rather than being ordinary auxiliary edges outside  $M$ .The distinction matters because the theorem explicitly treats doubled common edges as free closed components.4.4 What the explicit construction provesAssuming the stated coordinate lists are disjoint, the vertical and horizontal edges cover exactly the residual vertices, and the four paths alternate correctly with the original  $M$ , the construction gives
$$f_R^*\leq K+2.$$
Combined with the lower bound:
$$\boxed{f_R^*=K+2\quad(K\geq2).}$$
The conclusion is uniform in  $K$ . Nothing in the argument requires the HH path's actual edges to have zero physical weight; only their contribution to the TH objective is zero.The manuscript's stronger assertion that the unrestricted optimum is  $K+1$ , however, is not established by this retained-completion construction alone. It needs the independent unrestricted lower-bound and attaining-matching arguments from the original 12-by-18 construction. Those arguments must not be inferred from the residual Hall theorem.I would keep the two conclusions separate:Retaining  $A,C$ : exact cost  $K+2$ , from the new theorem and its extension certificate.Unrestricted: exact cost  $K+1$ , from the independent unrestricted argument.That distinction is necessary to make the claimed gap rigorous.5. Mandatory corrections and clarificationsI would require the following changes before treating the entire manuscript, including both numerical applications, as an independently self-contained exact result.LocationRequired changeReason§1Explicitly state that every auxiliary arc also has unit capacity.Makes the physical network specification unambiguous.§1Specify that residual sources and sinks cannot be internal vertices of directed paths.Makes the path-network correspondence precise.§1State the residual deletion convention for  $D_0$ , including removal of the selected entrance.Explains 17 rather than 18 black vertices.§2Explicitly quantify the lower bound over every full matching retaining all of  $R$ .Prevents accidental restriction to selected completions.§2Retain the maximum, never the sum.The two bounds charge the same additional expense.§3Express the attaining criterion with an existential quantifier over optimal physical path families.Failure of one optimizer's remainder test is inconclusive.§4Supply or cross-reference the exact original board matching and successful remainder matching.Makes the coordinate application independently reproducible.§5Include a disjointness/coverage certificate for the four paths, 42 vertical edges, 26 horizontal edges and 25 common edges.Edge counts alone do not prove a perfect matching.§5Distinguish common actual/auxiliary edges from ordinary auxiliary edges.Preserves the doubled-component convention.§5Cross-reference the independent unrestricted  $K+1$  proof.The retaining theorem does not establish the unrestricted optimum.Recommended strengthened statement of the exactness criterionThe cleanest formulation is:Theorem (physical compensation with direct-remainder attainment). Suppose  $C_s<\infty$ , and there exists an optimal family  $P$  of  $s$  vertex-disjoint TH paths from  $U$  to  $D$  such that the direct-remainder graph after fixing  $R\cup P$  has a perfect matching. Then
$$\boxed{f_R^*=b_R+C_s.}$$
Proof. The perfect matching gives  $f_R^*\leq b_R+C_s$ . The residual compensation theorem gives
$$f_R^*\geq b_R+\max(C_s,J_d)\geq b_R+C_s.$$
Equality follows.  $\square$ This formulation removes the redundant comparison hypothesis and avoids suggesting that the direct-remainder test characterizes all optimal completions.6. Final adjudicationGeneral residual Hall compensation theoremACCEPTThe all-completions quantifier, HH upper-capacity direction, physical vertex protection, endpoint relaxation, and maximum of the two lower bounds are correct.Attaining-completion criterionACCEPTCorrect as a sufficient certificate, not a necessary characterization. Clarify its existential optimizer quantifier.8-by-12 exact-four recoveryCONDITIONALCorrect application of the theorem given the separately established board and extension facts. No claim of a fresh coordinate-level audit.12-by-18 all- $K$  retaining constructionCONDITIONALThe Hall arithmetic, compensation logic and displayed edge counts are internally consistent. The full coordinate disjointness and coverage certificate still needs to accompany the construction.Unrestricted optimum  $K+1$ SEPARATE PROOFMust be supported independently, not attributed to the retained-path theorem.Overall: ACCEPT the mathematical theorem, with the specified presentation corrections. I find no defect in its central inequality or in the use of physical HH capacity. The principal contribution is the correct separation of endpoint Hall demand from physically realizable TH compensation, with both constraints charging the same residual expense.The scope limitation is also appropriate: this does not solve unrestricted TH optimization, prove coexistence of independently optimized flows, or turn a failed direct-remainder test into an infeasibility theorem.No checker execution, Lean verification, or independent reproduction of the two original board files is claimed.

ACCEPTI find no necessary mathematical or scope corrections in the supplied final revision. The residual lower bound is valid, the physical network has the required vertex capacities, and the attainment statement now has the correct existential quantifier. Both exact grid applications and both comparison controls check out from their coordinates.The corrected count in the weighted example is:StageBlack vertices in  $D_0$ Direct selected white neighboursBefore retaining-path deletion1718After deleting  $A,C$ 1716Both removed entrances,  $(6,15)$  and  $(9,12)$ , are white. No vertex of  $D_0$  is removed.This verdict concerns the supplied written mathematics and coordinate certificates. I did not execute the scripts or rely on the earlier acceptance verdict.1. General lower bound and physical capacityThe counting argument proves both boundsFix any retaining full matching  $N$ . In its residual terminal decomposition, let  $a_F,a_U,a_W$  count the paths ending in  $D$  whose sources belong to  $F,U,W'$ , respectively. Then
$$a_F+a_U+a_W=|D|,
\qquad a_F\le |F|,
\qquad a_W\le h_D.$$
Consequently,
$$a_U+a_W\ge d,
\qquad
a_U\ge \max(0,d-h_D)=s.$$
These inequalities supply precisely the two certificates used in §2:Choosing  $d$  paths with sources in  $U\cup W'$  gives a cardinality- $d$  endpoint matching. The assigned TH shortest-path costs are bounded above by the costs of the chosen physical paths, while HH assignments cost zero.Choosing  $s$  paths with sources in  $U$  gives a feasible family for the physical optimization defining  $C_s$ .The chosen families are subfamilies of actual residual terminal components. Their expenses are therefore bounded above by the entire additional TH expense, using nonnegativity. Thus, separately,
$$J_d\le f(N)-b_R,
\qquad
C_s\le f(N)-b_R.$$
This proves
$$b_R+\max\{C_s,J_d\}\le f_R^*.$$
The argument permits arbitrary additional TH and HH terminal paths. It does not require selected vertices to satisfy the colouring problem’s feasibility condition, and it does not require different paths to occupy different cores.The infeasibility conclusion also follows: a retaining completion would produce feasible witnesses for both relaxations. An infinite value in either relaxation therefore rules out such a completion.The stated arc capacities enforce vertex disjointnessThe capacity explanation in §§1–2 is correct. For each remaining actual edge  $bw\in M'$ , oriented  $b\to w$ :It is the unique outgoing physical arc of the black matched vertex  $b$ .It is the unique incoming physical arc of the white matched vertex  $w$ .Its unit capacity therefore bounds the total path flow through both endpoints. Two flow paths cannot share either endpoint without sharing this actual arc. Unit source and sink capacities protect terminal endpoints.A white  $Q'$  vertex cannot occur internally because it has no incoming physical arc. A black  $Q'$  vertex cannot occur internally because it has no outgoing physical arc. Thus the physical network does not allow a path to cross an intermediate terminal.Removing circulations from an integral flow preserves its value and cannot increase its cost. The resulting paths have the required physical disjointness. Conversely, any admissible disjoint path family induces such a flow. This establishes the claimed exactness for the  $s$ -path subproblem.There is also no missing terminal-path possibility from orienting actual edges only black-to-white: if an auxiliary matching uses an actual edge as a common edge, its two endpoints form a doubled closed component. Such an edge cannot simultaneously belong to a terminal component.Taking the maximum is essentialThe two relaxations charge portions of the same residual TH expense. Their proofs supply no disjoint allocation of expense between them. The use of
$$\max\{C_s,J_d\}$$
is therefore correct throughout, including the implementation description.The unit example supplies the promised concrete check: both values are two, and the total additional expense is two.2. The conditional attainment quantifier is correctSection 3 now makes the required assertion:There exists an optimal physical  $s$ -path family whose direct-TH remainder has a perfect matching.For such a family, deleting its vertices and those of  $R$  removes complete actual matched pairs from the interiors. Hence no surviving actual edge crosses the deletion.In the remaining graph, a selected terminal’s first auxiliary edge has only two possible types of black endpoint:A black  $Q$  endpoint, which terminates the component immediately.A black  $P$  endpoint, which begins a non-direct alternating terminal path.Forbidding the second type therefore makes every remaining TH path direct. Adding the fixed paths’ auxiliary edges to a perfect matching of this remainder produces expense exactly
$$b_R+C_s.$$
The lower bound then gives equality.The statement that success forces  $J_d\le C_s$  is also correct:
$$b_R+J_d\le f_R^*\le b_R+C_s.$$
No separate comparison hypothesis is needed.The failure interpretation is appropriately limited. A Hall obstruction in one chosen remainder rejects that choice of physical optimizer. It does not reject other optimizers or completions with further non-direct TH paths.The first comparison control reinforces this distinction: there  $C_s=1$  but  $f^*=K$ . For  $K\ge2$ , no optimal one-cost physical family can pass the direct-TH remainder test. That behaviour is fully consistent with §3’s certificate criterion.3. The  $8$ -by- $12$  retained-pair optimum is exactly fourThe supplied unit-board proof establishes the claimed values
$$b_R=2,\qquad d=1,\qquad h_D=0,\qquad s=1,
\qquad C_s=J_d=2.$$
Residual demand and HH exclusionThe original direct selected neighbourhood of the displayed seven black vertices is exactly the displayed eight-element set  $F$ . Retaining  $A,C$  removes the two selected sources
$$(4,9),\qquad (5,8),$$
and removes no vertex of  $D$ . The residual direct selected neighbourhood therefore has six vertices.I checked the stated HH reachability against the local actual matching. The reachable white states after deleting  $A,C$  are exactly
$$(4,5),\ (3,4),\ (2,3),\ (1,4),\ (2,5),\ (5,6).$$
The four core-0 states have no adjacency into  $D$ . At  $(5,6)$ , the possible continuation through the remaining graph cannot enter  $D$ : the relevant centre and the other onward matched black vertex have been removed, and an exterior black terminal cannot be crossed. Hence  $h_D=0$ .Two actual edges are necessary and sufficientThe one-edge obstruction is correct:The only white  $P$  vertices adjacent to  $D$  are  $(3,10)$  and  $(6,7)$ .The latter belongs to retained  $C$ .The actual mate of  $(3,10)$  is  $(3,11)$ .Its only white  $Q$  neighbour is  $(4,11)$ , which belongs to the direct neighbourhood  $F$ .Therefore a TH path from outside  $F$  into  $D$  cannot use zero or one actual edge. The displayed path
$$(0,11),(1,11),(2,11),(3,11),(3,10),(4,10)$$
uses exactly two and survives the retained-path deletion. It proves both  $C_s\le2$  and  $J_d\le2$ , completing the equality arguments.The attaining matching has complete coverageThe four displayed paths  $A,C,H,E$  are alternating and vertex-disjoint. Their auxiliary edges number
$$2+2+2+3=9,$$
and they use five of the twelve actual edges, leaving seven common  $M/N$  edges.The exterior row intervals are the actual complement of the deleted footprints, specified terminal endpoints, and eleven vertical edges. They contribute twenty-one horizontal edges. Thus the construction has
$$9+7+11+21=48$$
disjoint auxiliary matching edges and covers all  $96$  vertices.Its TH expense is  $1+1+2=4$ . The one actual edge on  $H$  is correctly free. Hence
$$\boxed{f_R^*=4}.$$
4. The weighted  $12$ -by- $18$  retained optimum is  $K+2$  for every  $K\ge2$ The corrected neighbourhood count is exactWith black parity  $r+c$  even, row 6 of the stated region has black positions  $(6,14),(6,16)$  and three white positions. Rows 7–11 contribute fifteen black and fifteen white positions.The direct selected neighbourhood of  $D_0$  before deletion is exactly the eighteen white positions in that region. Boundary neighbours outside the region that could matter are in  $P$ , rather than additional selected terminals. Deleting the two white entrances leaves sixteen selected neighbours and all seventeen black endpoints.For  $h_0=(3,5)$ , all four adjacent white vertices lie in  $P$ , so its direct selected neighbourhood is empty. Therefore the three demand values in §5 are correct:
$$d(D_0)=1,\qquad d(\{h_0\})=1,\qquad
d(D_0\cup\{h_0\})=2.$$
All three HH capacities are oneThere is only one residual HH source, so each capacity is at most one.A surviving HH path to  $h_0$  is
$$(6,7),(5,7),(5,6),(5,5),(4,5),(3,5).$$
The long displayed HH path supplies a surviving route to  $(10,12)\in D_0$ . Both avoid retained  $A,C$ . Consequently each of the three regions has  $h_D=1$ .For their union,  $d=2$  and  $h_D=1$ , so  $s=1$ . Every TH path from  $U$  into the union is non-direct and must use a residual actual edge. Both cheap edges have been removed with  $A,C$ ; every surviving actual edge has weight  $K$ . Hence
$$C_s\ge K.$$
The path
$$T_0:(0,5),(1,5),(2,5),(3,5)$$
attains this lower bound. For  $J_2$ , at most one assignment can use the HH source, and every TH assignment from  $U$  costs at least  $K$ . Assigning  $W$  to  $(10,12)$  and  $(0,5)$  to  $h_0$  attains  $K$ . Thus
$$\boxed{C_s=J_d=K}.$$
Looking at either region separately gives  $C_0=J_1=0$ , exactly as stated. The union detects the competition for the single HH source.The four paths coexist physicallyThe long HH path has eight actual edges, all belonging to the specified matching. Its nine other edges are auxiliary grid edges. Its vertices are distinct, and it avoids all vertices of  $C$ , including
$$(9,11),(9,10),(9,9),(9,12).$$
The other two TH paths lie in the other two square footprints, with distinct exterior sources.The actual-edge accounting is:One edge on  $A$ .One edge on  $C$ .One edge on  $T_0$ .Eight edges on the HH path.Thus eleven actual edges are used by the four paths, leaving twenty-five actual edges available as common  $M/N$  edges. In core 2 specifically, the unused actual edges are
$$(7,10)\!-\!(7,11),\quad
(8,10)\!-\!(8,11),\quad
(11,10)\!-\!(11,11),$$
which appear in the supplied  $N$ .The printed matching covers all  $216$  verticesI checked the supplied weighted edge list against the printed decomposition. The vertical table contains forty-two edges. The remaining horizontal intervals contribute twenty-six edges, and those intervals are the row-by-row complement of the stated deletions and vertical endpoints.The edge partition is therefore
$$\underbrace{15}_{\text{relay auxiliary}}
+\underbrace{25}_{\text{unused actual}}
+\underbrace{42}_{\text{direct vertical}}
+\underbrace{26}_{\text{direct horizontal}}
=108.$$
These categories are disjoint and cover the entire board. The expense is
$$1+1+K.$$
The HH path’s eight actual edges contribute zero to the TH objective.The lower and upper bounds use the same geometry for every stipulated integer  $K\ge2$ . They establish
$$\boxed{f_R^*=K+2}$$
for the whole stated range.5. The independent unrestricted  $K+1$  proof remains separate and validThe supplied source proof at revision fe425797 correctly establishes the weighted unrestricted comparison.There are three centres and only one HH source, so every full matching has at least two TH centre components. If a paid component uses a  $K$ -edge, a distinct TH centre component supplies at least one further unit of expense. This gives  $K+1$ .If no paid component uses a  $K$ -edge, the only possible TH centre relays are exactly the two displayed cheap relays. Their black entrance vertices each have the stated unique white  $Q$  neighbour. Both cheap edges are then occupied by those two components, the HH source must serve centre 0, and every other TH path must be direct. The  $17/16$  exterior deficit makes that impossible.The independent upper construction also checks. Its paths use four actual edges and seven auxiliary edges. The direct exterior tiling contains eight vertical and sixty-one horizontal edges. Together with thirty-two unused actual edges, this gives
$$7+32+8+61=108$$
edges and expense  $K+1$ .Thus the note correctly distinguishes
$$f_R^*=K+2
\quad\text{from}\quad
f^*=K+1.$$
The second equality has its own lower bound and attaining construction.6. Both comparison controls are correct, with the stated scopeThe  $4$ -by- $10$  control:  $J_d/C_s=K$ Both centres have empty direct selected neighbourhood, so  $d=2$ . The sole HH source reaches the right core. It cannot continue to the left core because doing so would require crossing an intermediate exterior terminal. Therefore  $h_D=1$  and  $s=1$ .A TH path to the right centre costs one, giving
$$C_s=1.$$
A cardinality-two endpoint assignment must cover the left centre. Its source must be TH, and its route costs at least  $K$ . Pairing the HH source with the right centre attains
$$J_d=K.$$
The printed attaining construction is valid. Its two relays contribute four auxiliary edges; six actual edges remain unused; the exterior matching has four vertical and six horizontal edges. Hence
$$4+6+4+6=20$$
edges cover the forty vertices, with TH expense  $K$ .The selected vertices have at most one  $P$ -neighbour, so this is indeed a feasible-selection control. It proves
$$f^*=K,\qquad \frac{J_d}{C_s}=K.$$
The  $6$ -by- $6$  control:  $C_s/J_d=(K+1)/2$ The sixteen actual edges cover all vertices except exactly the two stated white sources and two stated black destinations. Neither source is directly adjacent to either destination. Hence
$$d=s=2,\qquad h_D=0.$$
Both sources can enter the black endpoint  $(2,2)$  of the cheap actual edge. Its white endpoint  $(2,3)$  is adjacent to both destinations. Thus all four endpoint distances are one, and
$$J_d=2.$$
Two physical paths cannot share that actual edge. Since each path needs at least one actual edge, their combined expense is at least  $K+1$ . The two printed disjoint paths attain this amount. Their four auxiliary edges, together with the fourteen unused actual edges, form a full eighteen-edge matching. Therefore
$$C_s=f^*=K+1,
\qquad
\frac{C_s}{J_d}=\frac{K+1}{2}.$$
